title: The Impact of ChatGPT on English Language Learners’ Writing Skills: An Assessment of AI Feedback on Mobile
venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT-based mobile feedback can improve English as a second language (ESL) writing more effectively than traditional teacher feedback, with a particular focus on common grammatical errors and students’ attitudes toward AI-supported language learning. The study is motivated by the growing use of AI in education and the relative lack of direct empirical evidence comparing AI feedback with conventional classroom feedback in secondary ESL contexts.

The intervention was an eight-week quasi-experimental comparison between two intact groups. Students in the experimental group wrote 200-word picture-based stories, entered them into the ChatGPT mobile app, received AI feedback identifying and explaining grammatical and structural errors, and then revised their original stories accordingly. Students in the control group completed the same writing tasks but received feedback and grammar explanations from teachers before revising. Outcomes were measured with pre- and post-tests using picture-based writing tasks, and error analysis was conducted with Grammarly. A 12-item Likert questionnaire was also used to assess students’ attitudes toward using ChatGPT for grammar learning.

The participants were 132 twelfth-grade ESL students, aged 18 to 20, in a senior secondary public school in India. All were Hindi first-language speakers with more than 10 years of prior English study and familiarity with Android mobile use. The study was conducted in a classroom-based secondary school context, with the researcher serving as instructor for both groups.

The main findings indicate that the ChatGPT group showed significantly greater reduction in several grammatical error categories than the teacher-feedback control group, including present tense, past tense, progressive, past participle, plural, and possessive errors, though the control group performed better on comparative and superlative forms. Students also reported strongly positive attitudes toward ChatGPT, including ease of use, clarity of feedback, enjoyment, motivation, improved grammar understanding, and greater confidence in writing. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can serve as an effective supplement to traditional ESL instruction, especially for immediate, personalized feedback on writing accuracy, while noting the need for further research on longer-term effects and more adaptive feedback.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental comparative study in an adjacent priority population (senior secondary/Grade 12), with pre/post testing and a control group, but it uses convenience/purposive sampling, lacks random assignment, and reports limited detail on baseline equivalence and standardized outcome scoring.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest a modest-to-potentially substantial positive impact for a priority secondary population, especially on grammatical accuracy and writing confidence, but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes for the treatment contrast and the measured outcomes are narrower than overall writing quality.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT 3.5 mobile app provided conversational AI feedback on Grade 12 ESL students’ picture-based story writing, identifying grammar/structure errors, explaining them, and supplying examples for revision.
ChatGPT functioned as an AI writing feedback tool for error correction in secondary ESL writing, targeting inflectional and grammatical errors during revision of 200-word stories.

finding.finding_summary: Adjacent secondary evidence: In a quasi-experimental study in a senior secondary public school in India, Grade 12 ESL students (n=132; experimental n=66, control n=66) received either ChatGPT mobile feedback or traditional teacher feedback for 8 weeks. The ChatGPT group showed significantly fewer writing errors than the teacher-feedback group overall, with significant group effects (F(1,65)=13.745, p<.001), significant pre/post improvement (F(1,65)=123.676, p<.001), and a large overall effect across error categories (partial eta squared=.860 for error-type effects); gains were strongest for grammatical accuracy, while comparative and superlative errors favored the control group in some analyses.
finding.measure: Picture-based story writing pre/post tests; counts of grammatical/writing errors across present tense, past tense, progressive, past participle, plural, possessive, comparative, and superlative categories
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.860 (for main effect of error categories); no standardized between-group effect size reported

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT as an AI writing/language feedback tool on mobile was associated with improved ESL writing accuracy relative to teacher feedback in this Grade 12 quasi-experiment (n=132). The paper frames this as improved writing proficiency through reduction of common grammatical errors, but it does not report holistic writing-quality scores, revision-quality ratings, organization, evidence use, or style subscores.
finding.measure: Error reduction in revised 200-word narrative writing tasks scored via Grammarly-assisted error analysis

finding.finding_summary: Post-intervention survey responses from the 66 students in the ChatGPT condition indicated favorable attitudes toward AI feedback on mobile, with many students reporting improved motivation and confidence. For example, 68.18% strongly agreed they felt more confident in English writing after practicing with ChatGPT, 50.0% strongly agreed and 31.82% agreed they felt motivated to practice grammar regularly, and 74.27% strongly agreed they were satisfied overall.
finding.measure: 12-item Likert questionnaire on attitudes toward ChatGPT, including motivation, enjoyment, confidence in writing, satisfaction, and recommendation intentions
